summary: A 1969 proposal for the software a time-sharing host should include to use the network. It suggests system-level primitives available to user programs and a subsystem called Telnet, which would let a terminal at a remote host act like a terminal at the serving host.

plainLanguage.summary: This note suggests giving each big shared computer a toolkit so people can sit at one computer and use another far away as if it were next to them.

questions: network subsystem for time sharing hosts
subtitle: A 1969 proposal for Telnet, a small program that lets a terminal on one host act as a terminal on another.

tldr.problem: Time-sharing hosts would have network primitives for programs, but users also needed a convenient way to reach a remote host directly from a terminal.
tldr.mechanism: A subsystem called Telnet wraps the network system primitives so a teletype at one host acts as a teletype at the serving host, with a few commands such as CONNECT, LOGOUT and COPY FILE.
tldr.outcome: The author calls Telnet a level 0 network program that will quickly be surpassed, but simple enough to be working fairly soon.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 15 as Unknown and lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is the proposal that introduces the Telnet subsystem idea in September 1969, and the author expects it to be quickly surpassed.

sections.title: Primitives and the Need for Telnet
sections.content:
RFC 15 by C. Stephen Carr (University of Utah) builds on a set of network primitives proposed by G. Deloche of UCLA in NWG Note 11, to be included in each host's monitor system as system calls (SPOPs or BRSs on the 940, UUOs on the PDP-10). The primitives are: open primary connection, open auxiliary connection, transmit over connection and close connection.

In addition to program access, a convenient terminal route is wanted. The proposed subsystem, Telnet, is a shell program around those primitives that lets a teletype or similar terminal at one host function as a teletype at the serving host.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs already get a set of simple buttons. Telnet adds a way for a person at a keyboard to use them.

sections.title: The Telnet Subsystem
sections.content:
The Telnet code should fit in one core page, because it does very little. It sets up a shunt in the user host between the remote user and the serving host, and the connection leaves the user in the pre-logged-in state at the serving host. The commands are:

  • ESCAPE CHAR IS declares a character Telnet will watch for, so that text typed after it goes to Telnet instead of the serving host.
  • CONNECT TO takes the official site name (SRI, UTAH, UCLA, UCSB).
  • LOGOUT issues the logout sequence to the serving host.
  • COPY FILE moves a file over an auxiliary connection to the serving host.

Commands are accepted when Telnet is first entered or after the escape character.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet is a tiny pipe. It passes your typing along, except for a few special words you can say to Telnet itself.

sections.title: A Dialogue from Utah to SRI
sections.content:
The example has a user at Utah, logged in to the PDP-10, who wants the CAL subsystem on the 940 at SRI. They run Telnet, set an escape character, and connect to SRI. The connection is made provided SRI will accept another foreign user and the Utah user is cleared for network access. After logging in at SRI, characters are sent through the PDP-10 unchanged, and Telnet switches to full-duplex, character-by-character transmission because the 940 requires it.

The user then reads a CAL file from the pre-defined 940 name NETWRK, and, using the escape character and Telnet command, sends a PDP-10 file over an auxiliary connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A person at one computer dials into a faraway one, logs in, and even sends a file across without leaving their chair.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content: The author concludes that, given the basic system primitives, a Telnet subsystem at the user host and a manual for the serving host, the network can be employed profitably by a remote user. Telnet is described as a level 0 network program that will quickly be surpassed.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a simple first version. Better ones can come later.

references.text: Deloche, G., network primitives, NWG Note 11, 1969.
